concepts.title: Side chains set behavior
concepts.content: An amino acid's behavior is set by its side chain (R group), not the backbone every residue shares. Classifying the R group as nonpolar, polar uncharged, acidic, or basic predicts where a residue sits and what it can bond: hydrophobic side chains bury in the nonpolar core, polar and charged ones face the water.

problems.prompt: A residue is buried in the water-excluding core of a folded protein. What does that location predict about its side chain?
choices: It is a nonpolar hydrocarbon (e.g. leucine, valine)
It is acidic and negatively charged
It is basic and positively charged
It carries a polar hydroxyl that hydrogen-bonds water

problems.prompt: You must place a residue on a solvent-exposed loop that hydrogen-bonds with water. Which side chain fits?

concepts.title: Buffering peaks near pKa
concepts.content: A weak acid or base resists pH change most strongly when the ambient pH is near its pKa, where it is about half protonated and the Henderson-Hasselbalch ratio [A-]/[HA] is about 1. Distance from pKa is exactly what makes a group a poor buffer and leaves it nearly fully protonated or deprotonated.

problems.prompt: Titrating aspartic acid with NaOH, the curve flattens three times, each flat zone sitting at a pKa (about 2.0, 3.9, 9.9). Why does the pH barely move there?
choices: Buffering capacity peaks when pH is near pKa

problems.prompt: You need a side chain that shuttles protons at pH 7.4. Given aspartate (pKa 3.9), histidine (6.0), and lysine (10.5), which is best?
choices: Histidine, because its pKa is nearest 7.4
Any of them, since all are ionizable

concepts.title: Net charge and the isoelectric point
concepts.content: Net charge is fixed by where the ambient pH sits relative to a molecule's pKa values, summarized by the isoelectric point (pI): the pH at which positive and negative charges balance to zero net charge. Below pI a species is net positive, above pI net negative, and at pI it is neutral and least soluble.

problems.prompt: At pH 7.6, lysine (pI 9.7), aspartate (pI 2.8), and histidine (pI 7.6) are placed in an electric field. Which barely moves?
choices: Lysine, it runs to the cathode
Aspartate, it runs to the anode
Histidine, the running pH sits at its pI
They all migrate at the same speed

problems.prompt: To precipitate a protein out of solution you tune the buffer to its pI. Why does it aggregate there?
choices: It is most soluble at its pI
With zero net charge it stops repelling its neighbors
The pI maximizes the protein's charge

concepts.title: Amino-acid catabolism is nitrogen disposal
concepts.content: Amino-acid catabolism is fundamentally nitrogen handling: the alpha-amino group is first collected onto glutamate by transamination, then released as ammonium by oxidative deamination so it can be disposed of as urea, while the leftover carbon skeleton feeds central metabolism.

problems.prompt: Alanine aminotransferase moves alanine's amino group onto alpha-ketoglutarate, leaving pyruvate and glutamate. What has happened to the nitrogen?
choices: It has already been excreted as urea
It has only changed carriers (onto glutamate), not left
It has been oxidized to nitrate
It has been stored as a new amino acid

problems.prompt: Glutamate dehydrogenase then removes glutamate's amino group as free ammonium. What does this deamination accomplish?
choices: It liberates nitrogen for packaging into urea
It makes ATP directly from the amino group
It builds a nonpolar side chain

concepts.title: Each level is defined by its interaction
concepts.content: The levels of protein structure are defined by the kind of interaction at each tier, not by size: primary is the covalent sequence; secondary is local backbone hydrogen bonding (alpha-helices, beta-sheets); tertiary is one chain's three-dimensional fold from side-chain interactions; quaternary is the assembly of multiple chains.

problems.prompt: A mutation disrupts the regularly spaced backbone hydrogen bonds of an alpha-helix; the sequence and every side chain are unchanged. Which level is affected?
Each subunit of a four-subunit protein folds normally, but weakened contacts where the subunits meet let it fall apart into monomers. Which level?

concepts.title: Denaturation breaks the weak forces
concepts.content: Folding and denaturation turn on the weak, non-covalent forces (the hydrophobic effect, hydrogen bonds, van der Waals and ionic contacts) that hold a chain in its native fold. A denaturant disrupts those forces and unfolds the protein while leaving the primary sequence intact; whether function returns is just whether the chain re-finds the native state or gets trapped and aggregates.

problems.prompt: Adding 8 M urea abolishes a ribonuclease's activity; dialyzing the urea away restores it, and the peptide bonds were never touched. What happened?
choices: Non-covalent forces were disrupted, then re-formed
The active-site residues were chemically modified

problems.prompt: Heating the same enzyme past its melting point abolishes activity and the chains aggregate irreversibly. Why can heat denaturation fail to reverse when urea's did?
choices: Unfolded chains collide and aggregate instead of refolding
Heat attaches phosphate groups to the chain

concepts.title: Michaelis-Menten: Vmax and Km
concepts.content: Michaelis-Menten kinetics describes enzyme rate as a saturable, hyperbolic function of substrate concentration with two constants. Vmax is the ceiling reached when every active site is occupied, and Km, the substrate concentration giving half of Vmax, is an inverse measure of affinity (a lower Km means tighter binding).

problems.prompt: An enzyme's initial velocity climbs with substrate, then bends over to a plateau. What does the plateau represent?
choices: Vmax, with every active site occupied

problems.prompt: Enzyme X reaches half its maximum rate at 0.1 mM substrate; enzyme Y needs 2 mM. Which binds substrate more tightly?
choices: Enzyme Y, it needs more substrate
Enzyme X, it has the lower Km

problems.prompt: Two enzymes share a substrate. Reading only Km, what does a lower Km tell you?

concepts.title: Read the inhibitor type off Km and Vmax
concepts.content: A reversible inhibitor is identified by the pattern it leaves in Km and Vmax. Apparent Km up with Vmax preserved, and rescue by excess substrate, means the inhibitor competes at the active site (competitive). Vmax down with Km preserved, and no rescue, means it binds elsewhere (noncompetitive).

problems.prompt: With a drug present, Vmax is unchanged but apparent Km doubles, and flooding with substrate fully restores the rate. What kind of inhibition is this?
With a compound present, Vmax falls while apparent Km is unchanged, and excess substrate does not restore the rate. What kind of inhibition?
choices: The compound is just extra substrate

problems.prompt: For a competitive inhibitor, apparent Km = Km * (1 + [I]/Ki). If the apparent Km doubles, what is [I]?

concepts.title: The cell tunes its own enzymes
concepts.content: Enzyme regulation is the cell deliberately tuning an enzyme's activity to match its needs, distinct from an outside molecule merely competing for the active site: allosteric effectors at regulatory sites (often feedback inhibition of a committed step), cooperativity, and covalent modification such as phosphorylation.

problems.prompt: A pathway's end product binds the first committed enzyme at a site away from the active site, slowing it; as the product is used up, the enzyme speeds back up. This is:
A kinase attaches a phosphate to switch an enzyme between active and inactive forms, and a phosphatase removes it. This control is:
choices: A change in the primary sequence
